title: Title, date and publication
short: First printed in The Graphic, 29 December 1900, as 'By the Century's Deathbed'; collected in Poems of the Past and the Present (1901).
body: The poem appeared in The Graphic on 29 December 1900 under the title 'By the Century's Deathbed', and again in The Times on 1 January 1901, before Hardy collected it as 'The Darkling Thrush' in Poems of the Past and the Present (dated 1902 on its title page). The manuscript has '1899' struck out and '1900' written in: the nineteenth century strictly ended on 31 December 1900, though many had celebrated its end a year earlier. 'Darkling' (in the dark, at dusk) recalls Keats's nightingale and the 'darkling plain' of Arnold's 'Dover Beach'. Hardy was sixty at the time, and the elderly speaker is close to him.

sources.cite: The Victorian Web, 'The Darkling Thrush' (text, publication history, manuscript)

title: coppice
short: A coppice (copse) is a small wood of trees regularly cut back to the stump to produce poles; the gate leads into it.
body: Coppicing, the periodic cutting of hazel, ash or oak to the base so that it throws up new shoots, was a staple of the rural economy Hardy wrote about (compare the woodland trades of The Woodlanders). The word thus brings with it the idea of growth renewed after cutting, which the poem, at least at first, denies. Leaning on a gate is a characteristic posture of the rustic observer in Hardy.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'coppice'
Tim Armstrong, ed., Thomas Hardy: Selected Poems (Longman Annotated Texts, 1993), notes

title: Frost was spectre-gray
short: Frost personified, pale as a ghost; the first of the poem's images of death.
body: The capitalised 'Frost' and 'Winter' are personifications, in a style that recalls eighteenth-century and Romantic poetry. 'Spectre-gray' introduces the ghostly vocabulary that culminates in the century's 'corpse'. The spelling 'gray' is Hardy's. The landscape is presented as already haunted before the speaker meditates on the century's death, and the gray of frost anticipates the 'gloom' into which the thrush will sing. Hardy's adjectives throughout the first stanza (desolate, weakening, tangled, broken) build a cumulative sense of exhaustion that the bird's song will interrupt.

sources.cite: James Gibson, ed., Thomas Hardy: The Complete Poems (Macmillan, 1976), 'The Darkling Thrush' and textual notes
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'spectre'

title: Winter's dregs
short: The sediment at the bottom of a cup: winter's dregs are its last, most bitter remnants.
body: Dregs are the grounds left in a vessel after the liquid is drunk, and figuratively the worst or most worthless part. The image suggests a cup drained to the bottom, an end-of-the-line exhaustion that fits a dying century and the end of a December day. The dregs make 'desolate' the 'weakening eye of day', the sun low on the horizon.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'dregs'
Tim Armstrong, ed., Thomas Hardy: Selected Poems (Longman Annotated Texts, 1993), notes

title: eye of day
short: The sun, its light failing at dusk and in midwinter.
body: Calling the sun the eye of day is an old poetic figure (compare Shakespeare's 'the eye of heaven' in Sonnet 18). Here the eye is 'weakening', both as daylight fades at the dead end of the year, and the image of failing sight anticipates the speaker's own limited vision at the end: he is 'unaware'. The image also continues the personification of the season and the day.

sources.cite: Shakespeare, Sonnet 18, l. 5 ('the eye of heaven')
James Gibson, ed., Thomas Hardy: The Complete Poems (Macmillan, 1976), 'The Darkling Thrush' and textual notes

title: bine-stems
short: Bine is the flexible climbing stem of a plant such as hop or honeysuckle (woodbine); bare in winter, the stems scratch lines across the sky.
body: 'Bine' is a dialect variant of 'bind', used of the twining stems of climbers, as in 'hop-bine' and 'woodbine'. In midwinter only the tangled dead stems remain. 'Scored' means marked with lines or scratches, and also, with the lyre image that follows, written out as music: a score with nothing to play. The dead stems belong to the same world of plants regrowing after cutting as the coppice, here without visible renewal.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'bine'
Tim Armstrong, ed., Thomas Hardy: Selected Poems (Longman Annotated Texts, 1993), notes

title: strings from broken lyres
short: The stems look like the snapped strings of lyres: the instrument of poetry, especially Romantic poetry, now broken.
body: The lyre is the traditional emblem of lyric poetry; the Romantics favoured its cousin the Aeolian harp, played by the wind, as an image of the poet's inspired responsiveness (Coleridge's 'The Eolian Harp'; Shelley's 'Make me thy lyre' in 'Ode to the West Wind'). Hardy's lyres are broken: the winter wind finds no instrument to play, and the Romantic idea of nature inspiring song seems exhausted. The thrush will shortly contradict this.

sources.cite: P. B. Shelley, 'Ode to the West Wind' (1820), l. 57 ('Make me thy lyre')
S. T. Coleridge, 'The Eolian Harp' (1795/6)
Charles Lock, "'The Darkling Thrush' and the Habit of Singing", Essays in Criticism 36.2 (1986), 121-41

title: Stanza form
short: Four eight-line stanzas of alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter, rhymed ababcdcd: a hymn or ballad measure.
body: Each stanza doubles the common metre of hymns and ballads (8.6.8.6), with alternate rhymes. The form's familiarity from church hymnody suits a poem that borrows religious vocabulary ('evensong', 'carollings', 'blessed Hope') while doubting the faith it once expressed. The first stanza closes by withdrawing all humanity indoors ('all mankind that haunted nigh'), leaving the speaker alone with the landscape; 'haunted' continues the ghostly diction.

sources.cite: Tim Armstrong, ed., Thomas Hardy: Selected Poems (Longman Annotated Texts, 1993), notes
James Gibson, ed., Thomas Hardy: The Complete Poems (Macmillan, 1976), 'The Darkling Thrush' and textual notes

title: the Century's corpse outleant
short: The landscape as the laid-out body of the dead nineteenth century; 'outleant' is a Hardy coinage.
body: 'Outleant' (leant out, stretched out) is a rare compound of the kind Hardy favoured, and may be his own coinage. It suggests a corpse laid out for burial, and also a body leaning or projecting out over the land. The sharp features of the land are the corpse's features, emaciated in death. The image explains the original title, 'By the Century's Deathbed'. Readers differ on how far the dead century stands for a particular age (Victorian confidence, or the faith of earlier generations) or simply for time's passing.

sources.cite: Samuel Hynes, ed., The Complete Poetical Works of Thomas Hardy, vol. 1 (Clarendon Press, 1982), notes
James Gibson, ed., Thomas Hardy: The Complete Poems (Macmillan, 1976), 'The Darkling Thrush' and textual notes
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'outlean'

title: crypt ... canopy ... death-lament
short: The funeral of the century: the cloudy sky is its tomb, the wind its mourning song.
body: A crypt is an underground vault, usually beneath a church; a canopy is the cloth or structure held over a bier, throne or altar. The sky is thus both tomb and funeral pall, and the wind supplies the dirge. The whole scene is a secular funeral at which no one prays. The religious setting of a crypt anticipates the 'evensong' of the third stanza, where a service is finally sung.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'crypt'
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'canopy'
Tim Armstrong, ed., Thomas Hardy: Selected Poems (Longman Annotated Texts, 1993), notes

anchor: ancient pulse of germ and birth
title: germ
short: 'Germ' is the seed or rudiment from which life develops: the age-old rhythm of generation seems to have stopped.
body: 'Germ' (Latin germen, sprout) means the seed, bud or embryo; the 'pulse of germ and birth' is the rhythmic renewal of life in nature. Hardy had read Darwin closely, and the phrase gives biological life a pulse like a heartbeat, now 'shrunken hard and dry' like a dried seed. The image anticipates by contrast the 'aged thrush', in whom some life persists.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'germ'
Tim Armstrong, ed., Thomas Hardy: Selected Poems (Longman Annotated Texts, 1993), notes

title: fervourless
short: Without passion, warmth or zeal: the speaker projects his own spiritual coldness on to the world.
body: 'Fervour' (from Latin fervere, to boil) means intensity of feeling, and especially religious ardour. The line reveals that the desolation of the first two stanzas is partly the speaker's own; the landscape 'seemed' to be dead, and every spirit 'Seemed' as cold as he. That admission prepares for the surprise of the next stanza. The word also prepares the contrast with the 'ecstatic' bird.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'fervour'
Charles Lock, "'The Darkling Thrush' and the Habit of Singing", Essays in Criticism 36.2 (1986), 121-41

title: evensong
short: The service of Evening Prayer in the Church of England; the bird's song is likened to an evening service.
body: Evensong is the popular name for the Anglican Order for Evening Prayer. Hardy, who loved church music and had once considered ordination, gives the bird a liturgical role in a world from which the human worshippers have retired to their 'household fires'. 'Full-hearted' recalls Shelley's skylark pouring its 'full heart' in song. 'Illimited' (unlimited) is an older, more Latinate form.

sources.cite: Book of Common Prayer (1662), 'The Order for Evening Prayer'
P. B. Shelley, 'To a Skylark' (1820), ll. 1-5
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'evensong'

title: An aged thrush
short: Probably a mistle (missel) thrush, which sings in winter; the frail old bird mirrors the ageing speaker.
body: J. O. Bailey identified the bird as a mistle thrush, known for singing from treetops in winter weather. Unlike the 'immortal' nightingale of Keats or the skylark of Shelley, Hardy's bird is old, thin and storm-blown ('blast-beruffled'), so the Romantic singing bird is reimagined in the image of the poet himself, sixty in 1900. The adjectives emphasise how little physical cause the bird has for joy.

sources.cite: J. O. Bailey, The Poetry of Thomas Hardy: A Handbook and Commentary (U of North Carolina P, 1970), p. 166 (as cited by the Victorian Web)
The Victorian Web, 'The Darkling Thrush' (text, publication history, manuscript)
John Keats, 'Ode to a Nightingale' (1819), l. 51 ('Darkling I listen')

title: fling his soul / Upon the growing gloom
short: The thrush throws its whole being into song against the darkness; 'chosen' gives the bird an act of will.
body: 'Had chosen' attributes deliberate choice to the bird, as if its song were an act of defiance or faith. 'Fling' is reckless, wholehearted; 'soul' implies more than animal noise. The alliteration of 'growing gloom' marks the darkness against which the song is set, and returns to the idea of the darkling bird. The phrase contrasts with the passive humanity of stanza one, who 'had sought their household fires'.

sources.cite: Charles Lock, "'The Darkling Thrush' and the Habit of Singing", Essays in Criticism 36.2 (1986), 121-41
Tim Armstrong, ed., Thomas Hardy: Selected Poems (Longman Annotated Texts, 1993), notes

title: carollings
short: Joyful songs; at the end of December the word also suggests Christmas carols.
body: A carol was originally a ring-dance with song, and then a joyous song, especially one celebrating Christmas. The poem was published four days after Christmas, and the seasonal association adds to the religious vocabulary through which Hardy describes the bird. The speaker can see no 'cause' for such joy 'written on terrestrial things', that is, legible in the earthly world.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'carol'
James Gibson, ed., Thomas Hardy: The Complete Poems (Macmillan, 1976), 'The Darkling Thrush' and textual notes

title: terrestrial
short: Earthly things, as opposed to celestial ones: nothing on earth explains the bird's joy.
body: 'Terrestrial' (Latin terra, earth) carries a traditional contrast with the celestial (compare 1 Corinthians 15:40, 'There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial'). By locating the absence of cause in terrestrial things, the speaker leaves open, without asserting, the possibility of a cause beyond them. The Latinate word is also set against the plain monosyllables around it, a typical Hardyan mixture of learned and homely diction, and it raises the register at the moment the speaker reasons about causes. 'Afar or nigh around' insists that he has looked everywhere and found nothing.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'terrestrial'
Bible (KJV), 1 Corinthians 15:40

title: Some blessed Hope
short: The capitalised 'Hope' echoes 'that blessed hope' of Titus 2:13; critics divide over whether the ending is tentatively hopeful or ironic.
body: Titus 2:13 speaks of 'looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God'; Hope is also one of the three theological virtues (1 Corinthians 13:13). Hardy's 'Some' makes the Hope vague and conjectural, and 'I could think' makes it a possibility the speaker entertains rather than a belief. Some critics read the close as a cautious opening towards hope at the century's turn; others stress its irony, since the hope is attributed to a bird, whose song may be no more than instinct. Charles Lock has argued that the bird's singing may be habit rather than message.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), Titus 2:13
Bible (KJV), 1 Corinthians 13:13
Charles Lock, "'The Darkling Thrush' and the Habit of Singing", Essays in Criticism 36.2 (1986), 121-41

title: And I was unaware
short: The final admission of ignorance: the speaker cannot share or know the bird's hope.
body: The ending is quietly balanced. 'Whereof he knew / And I was unaware' grants the bird a knowledge the speaker lacks, but only within the hypothetical 'I could think'. The last word places the poet among the uncomprehending, consistent with the honest agnosticism of much of Hardy's verse. The poem stops short of conversion and of denial. Many readers find the poem's honesty in that refusal.

sources.cite: Charles Lock, "'The Darkling Thrush' and the Habit of Singing", Essays in Criticism 36.2 (1986), 121-41
Samuel Hynes, ed., The Complete Poetical Works of Thomas Hardy, vol. 1 (Clarendon Press, 1982), notes

title: December 1900
short: The date fixes the poem at the end of the nineteenth century; the manuscript first read 1899.
body: Hardy usually dated his poems, and here the date is part of the meaning: the 'Century's corpse' is the nineteenth century, which ended strictly at the close of 1900. The manuscript's deletion of '1899' (the year many celebrated as the century's end) has led some to suggest the poem was drafted then and redated for the true turn of the century.
